3.text: is well known among the American Eskimo. In Asia, however, it is used

4.text: chiefly with the broad snowshoes in walking on soft snow. When travelling

5.text: with netted snowshoes on hard ground, there is much less need for support.

6.text: The staff of this form is known through all the Arctic country of the Old

7.text: World as far west as Lapland.

8.text: Foot-racers and even herdsmen in the summer-time use a short staff

9.text: (Fig. 194, b), the lower end of which is tipped

10.text: with spikes made of antler. Often a couple of

11.text: nails serve for spikes. While running, the man

12.text: thrusts the staff as far ahead as possible, and

13.text: supports himself on it, trying to lengthen his

14.text: steps. Instead of this staff, runners will often

16.text: Another kind of staff is used in climbing

17.text: mountains. It has a head of antler or iron, with

18.text: two large, slightly curved spikes not unlike walrus-

19.text: tusks. These spikes are used for catching to rocks

20.text: in the most difficult places. This staff is used

21.text: mainly among the Kamchadal in hunting sheep

22.text: or bears on the rugged mountains. A similar

23.text: form is found among the Lamut hunters. I have also seen specimens among

24.text: those Chukchee of the Kolyma who live farther to the south.

25.text: Chukchee and Koryak, when walking over smooth ice, use ivory creepers

26.text: identical in shape with those of the American Eskimo (Fig. 195). These are

27.text: fastened to the sole crosswise to prevent slipping.
